prompt: What is the mean of the twelve orders, in reais, rounded to a whole number?
And the median of the same twelve orders, in reais?
hint: With twelve values, halfway between the sixth and the seventh once sorted.

prompt: Otávio wants to estimate what a thousand more orders like this week's would bring in. Which number should he use?
hint: A question about money, not about a typical customer.

choices.text: The median, R$ 305, because the mean is distorted by the hotel
choices.why: The median ignores how big the hotel's orders were, so revenue would be badly underestimated.

choices.text: The mean, R$ 2,607
choices.why: Right: total revenue divided by orders is what multiplies by a number of orders, provided the mix repeats.

choices.text: The mean without the hotel, R$ 304, as the honest figure
choices.why: Honest for households, but "orders like this week's" includes the hotel's.

choices.text: Neither: a forecast cannot use an average
choices.why: It can; the question is which average answers which question.

prompt: By the lesson, what was the real failure in the report that showed R$ 2,607?

choices.text: Using AVERAGE where MEDIAN was the correct function
choices.why: Both functions are correct; each answers a different question.

choices.text: Including business customers, who should never appear in sales data
choices.why: They are real sales; the lesson reports them on their own line, not out of the data.

choices.text: One number labelled "average ticket", read as typical
choices.why: Right: nobody looked at the rows behind it, and the label let the room assume what it described.

choices.text: Reporting a week, when a month would have averaged the hotel out
choices.why: A longer period dilutes the effect without telling anyone it is there.

prompt: What test does the lesson give for spotting a vanity metric?

choices.text: Whether it has grown every quarter
choices.why: Growth is a symptom of a cumulative total, not the test.

choices.text: Whether the marketing team chose it for a slide
choices.why: Who chose it does not decide what it can inform.

choices.text: If it doubled tomorrow, what would you do differently?
choices.why: Right: for registered customers the honest answer is nothing.

choices.text: Whether its data source can be audited by finance at the close
choices.why: A vanity metric can come from a perfectly auditable source.

prompt: Registered customers grew 12.8% in 2025 while active customers fell 5.6%. Why could the registered total not show the decline?
hint: What happens to an account when its owner stops buying?

choices.text: Accounts stay when people stop buying
choices.why: Right: it rises in a good year and a bad one alike.

choices.text: Because it is computed quarterly and the decline was monthly
choices.why: Active customers were measured quarterly too and showed it.

choices.text: Because it was rounded to the nearest hundred
choices.why: Rounding moves it by tens, not by thousands of departures.

choices.text: Because new accounts were counted twice
choices.why: Nothing says so; it would grow even counted perfectly.

prompt: A cumulative total such as app downloads since launch cannot ___, so every quarter is a record by construction.
Which of these are vanity metrics when reported as progress to Varanda's directors? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: App downloads since launch
choices.why: Right: a cumulative total that only grows.

choices.text: Customers who bought in the last 12 months
choices.why: It can fall, and in 2025 it did; that is what makes it worth reading.

choices.text: Page views since the site opened
choices.why: Right: it climbs whatever the business does.

choices.text: The returns rate
choices.why: A rate that moves both ways and points to something to fix.

choices.text: Social media followers
choices.why: Right: the actionable partner is orders that came from social media.

prompt: November 2025: 8,000 orders, 4,400 customers, 210 complaints. How many complaints per hundred orders, to one decimal?
Same month, same complaints. How many complaints per hundred customers, to one decimal?
Per order, complaints fell from 3.0 to 2.6; per customer, they rose from 3.8 to 4.8. Why do the two rates disagree?
hint: Divide orders by customers in each year.

choices.text: One of the two formulas has a mistake in it
choices.why: Both are correct arithmetic on the same columns.

choices.text: Complaints were counted differently in the two years
choices.why: Nothing in the data says so; the same 150 and 210 feed both rates.

choices.text: Each customer placed more orders: 1.82 against 1.25
choices.why: Right: more orders per customer means more chances for each customer to have a problem.

choices.text: The number of customers fell between the two Novembers
choices.why: Customers rose 10%; it is the orders per customer that changed most.

prompt: After paid campaigns were paused, visits fell 30%, orders fell 10% and conversion rose from 1.25% to 1.61%. What is the honest reading?

choices.text: The site got better at selling, so conversion is the news
choices.why: Nothing about the site changed; the visitors did.

choices.text: The data is wrong, because conversion cannot rise as orders fall
choices.why: It can: a rate rises when its denominator falls faster than its numerator.

choices.text: The keen visitors stayed; orders still fell
choices.why: Right: good news about the rate, not about the business.

choices.text: Paid campaigns hurt conversion, so they should stay off for good
choices.why: They cost 10% of orders; whether that is worth their price is a separate question.

prompt: Caio asks whether the warehouse and carriers handle an order well. Which complaint rate answers him?
hint: Count the chances for the thing being asked about.

choices.text: Complaints per customer
choices.why: That answers how many people had a bad experience, a different question.

choices.text: Complaints per order
choices.why: Right: every order is a chance to fail, and on that measure it improved.

choices.text: The count of complaints, which rose 40%
choices.why: A count with no denominator answers neither question.

choices.text: Complaints per visit to the site
choices.why: Most visits are not orders; they give no chance for a delivery to fail.

prompt: Contagem delivered 300 of 400 furniture orders and 95 of 100 parcels on time. What is its on-time rate for all deliveries, in percent?
Contagem is ahead of Savassi with furniture and with parcels, yet behind in the total. Why?

choices.text: The totals were computed with a different formula from the parts
choices.why: Same formula; the totals simply weight the parts by each store's own mix.

choices.text: Most of its deliveries are furniture, the hard kind
choices.why: Right: its total leans towards its furniture rate, Savassi's towards its parcel rate.

choices.text: Savassi is better and the per-kind rates are noise
choices.why: With 100 to 400 deliveries per row, five points in both kinds is not noise.

choices.text: Contagem delivers more in total, and bigger stores do worse
choices.why: Both stores made 500 deliveries; size is not the difference.

prompt: Put the checks before ranking two groups on a total in the lesson's order.
hint: Total, then the rows, then why they differ, then a fair comparison.
items: Break it down by the part that is hardest to do well
Look at each group's mix of parts
Compare the groups on a common mix
trap: Choosing a common mix before seeing the mix of each group is fixing a problem you have not yet found.

prompt: Two carriers: Rota Sul is on time 88% overall, Expresso Norte 81%. Expresso Norte does most of the rural routes, which are late for everybody. What should Caio check before moving routes to Rota Sul?
hint: The same table with other nouns.

choices.text: Nothing: seven points is a clear gap
choices.why: Contagem had a seven-point gap too, and it measured the mix.

choices.text: The price each carrier charges per delivery
choices.why: Price matters to the decision, but it does not tell him which carrier is better at delivering.

choices.text: Rural and urban rates, separately
choices.why: Right: if Expresso Norte wins both rows, its total is measuring its mix of routes.

choices.text: Whether the rural routes should be dropped
choices.why: That is a different decision; the comparison has to be fixed first.

prompt: The delivery KPI went from 76.9% to 86.2%. By how many percent did it rise, relative to where it started, to one decimal?
Complaints about the solar lamps went from 1 to 3, "up 200%", on twelve units a month. What does the lesson make of it?
hint: How many more complaints is it?

choices.text: Pull the range: 25% of units drew a complaint
choices.why: On twelve units one customer moves the rate by more than eight points; that is too little to act on.

choices.text: Two more complaints: keep watching, and show the count beside the rate
choices.why: Right: twelve units cannot separate a faulty product from bad luck.

choices.text: The 200% is wrong; it is really 300%
choices.why: From 1 to 3 is a 200% rise; the arithmetic is fine.

choices.text: Nothing, because complaints are not a KPI
choices.why: Whether it is a KPI does not change how to read a rate on twelve cases.

prompt: Conversion going from 1.25% to 1.5% is a rise of 0.25 percentage ___, or 20 percent.
hint: The unit of a difference between two percentages.

prompt: Match each misleading number to what the lesson puts back beside it.
hint: Each misleads by what it leaves out.

pairs.left: An average ticket pulled up by two orders
Registered customers, a record every quarter
A return rate of 25% on twelve units

prompt: Renata's slide says "conversion up 20%". In points, it went from 1.25% to 1.5%. What should the slide say?
hint: Points for a difference, percent for a relative change.

choices.text: Nothing different: 20% is correct
choices.why: It is correct and incomplete; alone it is the truth in its most flattering form.

choices.text: "Conversion up 0.25%"
choices.why: That calls a difference in points a percent, which is wrong.

choices.text: "Up 0.25 points, from 1.25% to 1.5%, a 20% rise"
choices.why: Right: both, each with its unit, and the two levels.

choices.text: "Conversion up 20 points"
choices.why: That would be from 1.25% to 21.25%.

prompt: Sônia reports turnover of 40% a year in the garden department at Betim, the highest of any team. The department has five employees and two left. What should Lívia propose before the number reaches Helena?

choices.text: To show it as "2 of 5" and keep it out of the ranking
choices.why: Right: on a base of five, one person moves the rate by twenty points.

choices.text: Whether the formula used the right denominator
choices.why: The denominator is right; it is just tiny.

choices.text: Whether the median turnover would be lower than the mean
choices.why: There is one rate here, not a list of values to summarise.

choices.text: Whether turnover is a vanity metric
choices.why: Turnover can fall and points to action; the problem is the base, not the kind of number.

prompt: A report says "returns fell 15% in March". Orders fell 30% the same month. Which reading is the lesson's?

choices.text: Good news: fewer returns means better products
choices.why: Fewer orders means fewer chances to return; the count fell less than its base.

choices.text: No reading is possible without a full year of data
choices.why: One month is enough to compute a rate, which is the missing step.

choices.text: Returns and orders are unrelated, so both are fine
choices.why: Returns come from orders; that is the denominator.

choices.text: The rate got worse, as its base fell faster than the count
choices.why: Right: the bare count hid a worse rate.
